title: Erratic Glucose and Lumpy Injection Sites / Feel the Skin Before You Change the Dose

blocks.text: Erratic Glucose and Lumpy Injection Sites / Feel the Skin Before You Change the Dose

AMaC MRCP PACES · R5-261 · Consultation · PACES Station 5, less acute consultation · Skills A–G (all seven) · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, 5 with the examiners) · Guidelines: NICE NG17, Type 1 diabetes in adults (published 26 August 2015; last updated 17 August 2022; reviewed 30 January 2026, recommendations unchanged) · Related AMaC: new type 1 diabetes communication station; SGLT2 inhibitor ketoacidosis station

Dear Doctor, Mr Dylan Hargreaves, 38, parcel delivery driver. Type 1 diabetes for 22 years, on basal–bolus insulin by pen, with a flash glucose sensor. His glucose swings widely with no clear pattern, and his HbA1c has risen from 58 to 71 mmol/mol over a year. He reports two low-glucose episodes last month. The practice nurse noted lumps on his abdomen but did not examine further. No other regular medicines. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mr Hargreaves.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: HOOK: In erratic type 1 control the skin is the first investigation; lumps that release insulin unpredictably are found by touch, not assumed.

TRAP: He asks you to raise his insulin for the evening highs. Given into the same lumps, it arrives late and worsens the early-hours lows. Pass: examine, explain, then move sites on lower agreed doses. Fail: raise the dose, or move sites at full dose.

rows: Think
Say
Do
Erratic highs and lows in a daily injector: sites and technique come before any dose change.
“Tell me where you inject, what happens to the needle afterwards, and at what times the swings hit.”
Sites, rotation, needle reuse, pen storage, timing of lows and highs, awareness of lows, sensor alarms, work and driving.
The lumps are the key sign; he may be embarrassed, so protect his dignity.
“May I look at and feel those areas? I can ask a chaperone to join us.”
Wash hands, consent, expose the abdomen only, inspect, palpate with flat fingers, compare with the thighs, cover him.
Fresh skin absorbs insulin fully, so the same dose may cause a low, especially asleep.
“The lumps trap insulin. Moving helps, but your doses will need to come down first.”
Name the diagnosis, give the options with benefits and risks, ask his choice, involve the diabetes team on doses.
He drives for a living and fears for his licence; tonight must be safe.
“Let us go through tonight, and what you will do if you wake sweaty.”
Group 1 driving advice, glucose check before driving, sensor low alarm on, fast carbohydrate, review this week, teach-back.

History of sites and swings
Asks about HbA1c and doses only; never asks where, how often or with what he injects.
Asks which sites he uses, whether he rotates, how long each needle is kept, and when highs and lows happen.
Adds needle length, pen storage and sensor alarms, and links evening highs and 3 a.m. lows to the abdominal sites.

A, B
Examining the sites
Does not inspect or feel the injection sites, or reports them normal.
Asks consent, exposes the abdomen only, inspects then palpates with flat fingers, and reports firm, rubbery, non-tender swellings beside the umbilicus.
Compares with surrounding skin and thighs, estimates size, checks for bruising, redness and warmth, and notes injection marks clustered within the lumps.
R3
D
Differential diagnosis
Blames poor control or diet; does not link the lumps to erratic glucose.
Names lipohypertrophy from repeated injection and needle reuse, explaining that insulin is absorbed unpredictably from it.
Also weighs cutaneous amyloidosis, missed doses, heat-damaged insulin and gastroparesis, and says why trapped insulin fits his pattern best.
R4

His fear about work
Ignores his cues about work, or promises he will be fine before knowing what he fears.
Asks how this affects work and driving, and acknowledges his fear about his licence when he voices it.
Asks what he fears most, answers with the actual position rather than a promise, and explains why honesty protects his licence.

E, C
Shared decision on moving sites
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): switches him to new sites at full dose without warning of hypoglycaemia.
Offers moving now on reduced doses, moving once the team agrees doses, or carrying on; names the overnight risk; asks his choice.
Sets the overnight-hypoglycaemia risk against his own pattern, covers staying put, checks the choice fits his home routine, and records it.
R6
G
Welfare and safety
Exposes him without asking or leaves him uncovered; tells him to carry on driving as normal.
Offers a chaperone, asks about pain, covers him afterwards; advises testing before driving, not driving when low, and carrying fast-acting carbohydrate.

States the Group 1 position: lows in sleep do not count unless he cannot recognise lows; two or more severe lows while awake in 12 months, or any severe low while driving, means stop driving and notify DVLA; test before and during journeys; carry a finger-prick meter as sensor backup.

E
Plan and timescale
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): raises the insulin doses to chase the highs.
Stops injecting into lumps, rotates sites, uses a new needle each time, and arranges team review this week with a dose plan and extra checks.
Gets doses agreed before the first fresh-site injection, sets a bedtime check and the sensor low alarm, and plans a site check at each review.

C
Explanation and understanding
Uses unexplained terms such as lipohypertrophy and absorption, and ends without checking he has understood.
Explains in plain words that the lumps trap insulin so it arrives unpredictably, then summarises the plan.
Uses teach-back: asks him to say what he will do tonight and what he will do if he wakes sweaty.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.

Who you are. You are Dylan Hargreaves, 38, a parcel delivery driver, with type 1 diabetes since 16. You live with Kelly, your partner, and your four-year-old daughter. You are guarded and expect a telling-off.
Opening line. “My sugars are all over the place, doctor, and nobody can tell me why.”

You volunteer. Highs after your evening meal. Some nights you wake around 3 a.m., sweaty. Last month Kelly found you muddled and gave you orange juice. One afternoon your sensor read 2.6 while parked on a delivery; you ate sweets.

Only if asked. You inject only into your tummy, either side of the belly button; the lumpy bits hurt less and your thighs feel sore. The lumps are a year or two old. One needle stays on for about a week; the van has no sharps bin. You take insulin degludec 22 units at 10 pm and insulin aspart 6 to 10 units with meals, plus extra to correct highs. You skip lunchtime insulin when busy. You scan a flash sensor six to eight times daily, never before driving; its low alarm is off as it woke Kelly. You feel lows at about 3.5, shaky and sweaty; the afternoon one crept up. Spare pens live in the van door.
Background. Medicines: ibuprofen now and then. Allergies: none. Never smoked. Alcohol: eight units weekly. Travel: none abroad this year. Family: father type 2 diabetes; mother underactive thyroid.

Hidden concern. You fear losing your licence and job. Say so only if asked what worries you, or about work or driving. If not asked by ten minutes: “Is this going to affect my job?” Then: “If I tell you about the lows, does it go straight to DVLA? I told them when I started insulin. The van pays our rent.”
Your questions. “Can’t you just put my insulin up?” “Do you have to look?” “If I use my legs, will I be all right at night?” “Do I have to stop driving?”

How you react. Good handling (kind, clear, offers choices): you relax, admit the reuse and skipped doses, and choose to switch straight away on reduced doses, with the alarm back on. You first want to start tonight; once the night risk is explained, you want the nurse to set doses first. Poor handling (lecture, false reassurance, more insulin): you go quiet and say, “Fine, I’ll start with my legs tonight.”
Findings, released as each step is done
Observations asked: Pulse 76 regular, blood pressure 128/78, afebrile, capillary glucose 7.9 mmol/L.
Abdomen exposed and inspected: Two raised swellings either side of the umbilicus; normal skin colour; no scar, redness or ulcer.
Palpation: Right about 7 × 5 cm, left 4 × 4 cm; firm, rubbery, non-tender, not warm; puncture marks and two old bruises within. Surrounding abdomen, thighs, buttocks normal.
Sensor report asked: Fourteen days: 2.6 to 19.8 mmol/L; evening highs; lows 02:00 to 05:00 on six nights.
Question ladder
Q1 [R3] EXAMINER: “What explains his erratic control?” MODEL: Lipohypertrophy at overused abdominal sites with needle reuse: erratic absorption gives evening highs and delayed night lows.
Q2 [R3] EXAMINER: “What else would you consider?” MODEL: Cutaneous amyloidosis, missed or mistimed doses, heat-damaged insulin, gastroparesis.

Q3 [R5] EXAMINER: “What is the risk of moving sites?” MODEL: Absorption becomes complete, so the usual dose can cause hypoglycaemia, especially asleep. Agree lower doses with the diabetes team; monitor closely.
Q4 [R7] EXAMINER: “What injection advice do you give?” MODEL: Rotate, avoid the same point, use a new needle every time, consider another length, and arrange regular site checks.

Q5 [R6] EXAMINER: “What do you tell him about driving?” MODEL: He holds a Group 1 licence and has notified DVLA. Separate lows in sleep from severe lows while awake, advise glucose checks around journeys, and say when to stop driving and notify.
Curveball: He says he will start his thighs tonight at full doses. Safe answer: do not; agree reduced doses first, or contact the diabetes team or out-of-hours service today.
Establishes which areas he injects, whether he moves around, and how often the needle is changed (C)
Asks about the timing of highs and lows and connects the pattern to the injection areas (C, D)
Seeks consent, offers a chaperone, uncovers only the abdomen and covers him afterwards (G)
Looks before touching, uses the flats of the fingers, and contrasts with normal skin and the thighs (A)
Describes the lumps as rubbery and painless, one each side of the navel, with no sign of infection (B)
Names lipohypertrophy and explains the unreliable insulin delivery (D, C)
Asks what he fears and picks up the cue about work and his licence (F)
Lays out three options, including no change, with the overnight risk of fresh sites (E)
Declines to raise doses; plans lower doses, agreed with the team, for the very first injection into healthy skin (E)
Gives accurate driving advice for an insulin-treated Group 1 licence (G, E)
Uses teach-back for tonight and for waking sweaty (C)
Fail
CANDIDATE: Your HbA1c has crept up. How much insulin are you taking? [R1 Fail]
PATIENT: Twenty-two at night and my mealtime doses. My glucose is a rollercoaster.
CANDIDATE: The nurse already noted the lumps, so I will not examine them. [R2 Fail] This is just poor control. [R3 Fail]
PATIENT: Will this cost me my job?
CANDIDATE: You will be fine. [R4 Fail]
PATIENT: Can’t you put my insulin up?

CANDIDATE: Yes, increase it, and use your thighs from tonight on the same doses. [R5 Fail] [R7 Fail] Keep driving exactly as before. [R6 Fail] The lipohypertrophy is causing glycaemic variability. [R8 Fail]

EXAMINER NOTE: The lumps were never felt, the diagnosis was missed, and the fear went unanswered. Raising doses and moving sites at full dose is unsafe: absorption from fresh skin is complete, so a night-time low is likely.
Pass
CANDIDATE: Where do you inject, do you rotate, and how long is each needle kept? [R1 Pass] When do the highs and lows come? [R1 Pass]
PATIENT: Only my tummy. A needle lasts a week. Highs after tea, lows around 3 a.m.
CANDIDATE: May I look and feel? A chaperone can join us; tell me if anything hurts. [R2 Pass] [R6 Pass]
PATIENT: Just you is fine.
CANDIDATE: [Uncovers only the tummy; looks, then feels flat-fingered.] The lumps beside the navel, one each side, are firm, rubbery, non-tender. [R2 Pass] I will cover you now. [R6 Pass]

CANDIDATE: This is lipohypertrophy: fat thickened by repeated injections and reused needles. It traps insulin, so each dose absorbs unevenly. [R3 Pass] [R8 Pass] How are the lows affecting work and driving? [R4 Pass]
PATIENT: Will DVLA hear about this? The van is my livelihood.
CANDIDATE: That sounds worrying. [R4 Pass] We could move now on lower doses, which settles the swings but needs care overnight; move once the nurse sets doses; or carry on. Which suits you? [R5 Pass]
PATIENT: Start tonight, with the lower doses.

CANDIDATE: So: no injections into the lumps, rotate sites, a fresh needle every injection, nurse review this week for doses and extra checks. [R7 Pass] [R8 Pass] Test before driving, never drive low, keep fast sugar handy. [R6 Pass]
EXAMINER NOTE: Safe: examined, explained, offered choices, no dose rise. Licence rules not stated; nothing tested back.
High-Performance

CANDIDATE: Is it always the tummy, or have you tried your thighs? What needle length, where are your pens kept, does your sensor alarm at night? Post-tea highs and early-hours lows may both come from that patch. [R1 High]

CANDIDATE: [Chaperone offered, pain asked about, only the abdomen uncovered. Palpates flat-fingered, comparing with the thighs.] Right swelling about seven by five centimetres, left four by four, clustered needle marks and old bruises, no redness or warmth. [R2 High] [Covers him.]
CANDIDATE: This is lipohypertrophy. Amyloid lumps, skipped doses, insulin spoiled by heat and slow stomach emptying are possible, but trapped insulin fits your pattern best. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: What worries you most about this? [R4 High]
PATIENT: Losing my licence. I’ve got a little girl.

CANDIDATE: You are not being punished for telling me; open reporting protects your licence. [R4 High] On a car licence, a low in your sleep does not count unless you cannot feel lows coming. Two or more severe lows while awake in a year, or any severe low at the wheel, mean stopping and telling DVLA. Test before you set off and at least every two hours; keep a spare finger-prick meter with the sensor. [R6 High]

CANDIDATE: Your lows cluster between 2 and 5 a.m., so moving now settles the swings but risks a night low; waiting is safer tonight; staying put leaves both. Does Kelly’s night routine change what suits you? I will note your choice. [R5 High]
PATIENT: Move now. Kelly can keep an eye on me.

CANDIDATE: The diabetes team will set your doses before the first thigh injection; your sensor alarm goes back on, with a bedtime check. [R7 High] Tell me what you will do tonight, and if you wake sweaty. [R8 High]
EXAMINER NOTE: Specific, prioritised and ahead of the next question: the fear was named, the licence position stated, and the plan set before any injection into healthy skin.
R2: Takes the lumps from the letter and does not feel them. The examiner sees no technique and no signs found, so Skills A and B stay undemonstrated.
R5: Moves him to fresh sites at his usual doses. The examiner sees a red flag: fresh skin takes up the full dose, which can bring a low while he sleeps.
R7: Raises insulin to chase the evening highs. The examiner sees a red flag: the lumps then release the extra insulin late and deepen the 3 a.m. lows.
R4: Promises he will keep his licence before hearing his story. He may stop being open about his lows, and the promise may prove false.
R6: Leaves the abdomen exposed while talking and asks nothing about pain. Skill G is judged throughout the encounter, not only at the end.
“I have not yet felt those areas; may I examine them before I explain?”
“Before we change any dose, I want to avoid trading erratic highs for night-time lows.”
“I cannot promise what DVLA will decide, but I can tell you what the rules say for your licence.”

Lipohypertrophy is a firm, rubbery swelling of fat at sites injected repeatedly or with reused needles; insulin absorbed from it is unpredictable. Cutaneous amyloidosis can look the same (Diabetes UK). NICE NG17: advise rotating sites and avoiding the same point (1.7.19); offer other needle lengths if there are problems (1.7.17); check sites at least annually and whenever control changes (1.7.21); in erratic control, consider technique and sites before changing an optimised regimen (1.7.22). On moving to healthy tissue, reduce the dose with the diabetes team and monitor closely; the size is per local protocol. DVLA: severe means needing another person’s help. For Group 1, lows during sleep are not relevant unless he cannot recognise lows; two or more severe lows while awake in 12 months, or any severe low while driving, means stop driving and notify DVLA. Group 2 must report all severe lows, including in sleep. Sensor users must carry a finger-prick meter as backup. Low-glucose alarms should be set above 4.0 mmol/L; a driver who relies on alarms to detect lows must stop driving and notify DVLA.
THINK: Lumps trap insulin; fresh skin at full dose risks a night low.
SAY: “Before I change any dose, I need to examine your injection sites.”
DO: Consent, chaperone; inspect, palpate; ask sites, needles, timing; driving.
NUMBERS: 1 cm between injections (Diabetes UK, content dated 2 October 2025); annual site check (NG17 1.7.21).
TRAP: Putting the dose up, or switching sites at full dose.
FINISH: Stop using the lumps; team-set lower doses; monitoring; review this week.

NICE NG17, Type 1 diabetes in adults: diagnosis and management (published 26 August 2015; last updated 17 August 2022; reviewed 30 January 2026, recommendations unchanged) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng17 — supports recommendations 1.7.17, 1.7.19, 1.7.21 and 1.7.22 and the hypoglycaemia-awareness section. Accessed 16 October 2026.

DVLA, Diabetes mellitus: assessing fitness to drive (last updated 7 November 2025) — https://www.gov.uk/guidance/diabetes-mellitus-assessing-fitness-to-drive — supports the definition of severe hypoglycaemia, the Group 1 and Group 2 positions, glucose testing around journeys, and sensor use with a backup meter. Accessed 16 October 2026.

Diabetes UK, Injecting insulin (content dated 2 October 2025) — https://www.diabetes.org.uk/about-diabetes/looking-after-diabetes/treatments/insulin/injecting — supports lipohypertrophy and cutaneous amyloidosis, injecting at least 1 cm from the last site, and never reusing needles. Accessed 16 October 2026.

Clinical Diabetes 2019;37(3), “The Injection Technique Factor: What You Don’t Know or Teach Can Make a Difference” — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640874/ — Supplementary source (US review); supports lowering the dose when moving from lipohypertrophic to normal tissue with close glucose monitoring. Accessed 16 October 2026.
